$comment: Registry of upstream constants and logic this client mirrors by hand.
An entry belongs here when BOTH are true:
1. The value drives a client-side DECISION (what to send, what to show, what to allow).
2. The server never serves it, so drift cannot be detected at runtime.
Type-shape mirrors (data classes tracking upstream response types) do NOT belong here:
they are self-correcting, because a wire change surfaces as a decode failure or a null
field. The entries here fail SILENTLY -- the app keeps running and quietly makes worse
Read by scripts/check-mirrors.py, which diffs each watched region between two upstream
revisions during a /sync-upstream pass. Adding a mirror to the codebase means adding it
mode: 'block' watches one anchored declaration; 'file' watches a whole upstream file,
for mirrors that are spread across it rather than living in a single table.

entries.why: The concrete MIME types the native file picker filters on. Transcribed verbatim, in upstream order, so the two lists stay diffable.
entries.failure_mode: A type upstream added is absent from the picker, so the user cannot select a file the server would have accepted. No error -- the file simply isn't offered.

entries.why: Upstream spreads this into fullMimeTypesList; the Kotlin transcription inlines it, so a change here does not show up as a change to fullMimeTypesList.
entries.failure_mode: Same as full-mime-types-list, and easier to miss because the upstream diff touches a different symbol than the one the Kotlin file names.

entries.why: Which providers can take a document natively. The router sends a file to server-side text extraction only when the provider is absent from this set, so membership decides the delivery mode. Note the commented-out azureOpenAI entry is load-bearing -- it records a deliberate exclusion, so a comment-only change here is still a real change.
entries.failure_mode: A provider upstream ADDED keeps having its documents extracted to text instead of sent natively -- worse quality, no citations, no error. A provider upstream REMOVED gets documents sent natively that it cannot read, which is the silent drop this feature exists to fix. This set changed four times in the 4.6 months after it was introduced, at gaps of 8, 4, 6 and 3 weeks.

entries.why: Bedrock's own document allowlist, which is broader than the image+PDF set every other document-capable provider gets. Keyed by MIME type; upstream's values are extensions used only for Converse's format field.
entries.failure_mode: A Bedrock-supported type is routed to text extraction rather than sent natively, or an unsupported one is sent natively and rejected at send.

entries.why: The server normalises these on receipt, but the router runs first, so the client must apply the same aliasing before any table lookup.
entries.failure_mode: An un-aliased type misses every lookup and falls through to the provider path. Concretely: without the text/x-markdown alias a .md file mis-routes on Bedrock.

entries.why: The types the built-in document parser can extract without an OCR service configured. This is the half of the routing rule that says the server can demonstrably read the file; whether OCR is configured is server-side only and not exposed on any config endpoint, which is why the whitelist is the gate.
entries.failure_mode: A type upstream added to the parser is never routed to text, so it stays on a provider that cannot read it. A type upstream removed is routed to text and returns a generic 500.

entries.why: Decides whether a tool call's generated file renders as an inline image preview or as a download chip, for the attachments that arrive with no MIME type. The exclusions are load-bearing: svg is absent upstream, and an .svg the server extracted text for is meant to reach the artifacts panel instead, so 'completing' this list is itself the drift.
entries.failure_mode: An extension upstream added renders as a download chip instead of an image the user can see. One removed sends a non-image down the image path, where a null resolved URL degrades it to a chip. Neither errors.

entries.why: The reason keys the feedback route accepts, and the rating each one belongs to. The route re-checks the pairing and rejects a mismatch with 400.
entries.failure_mode: A removed or re-directed key is still offered in the picker; submitting it 400s. A newly added reason is silently unavailable.

entries.why: The artifact mode values sent to the server as a generation parameter.
entries.failure_mode: An unknown mode is sent, or a newly supported one is unreachable from the client.

entries.why: Which generation parameters each endpoint, provider and Bedrock variant exposes, along with their ranges and defaults. Mirrored across the whole Kotlin registry rather than as one table, so the watch is file-level.
entries.failure_mode: A parameter is offered with a stale range or default, or a newly supported one is missing. Values outside the server's accepted range are rejected at send time.

entries.why: Ported in shape from findArtifactClose/getOpeningCodeFence. The real contract is 'whatever micromark parses', so this is a behavioural port, not a table. Three divergences are deliberate and pinned by ArtifactDetectorCorpusTest. Only the DETECTION half of update.ts is mirrored: replaceArtifactContent and the normalizeBeforeClosingArtifactFence it calls run server-side when an artifact-edit tool rewrites a message, so their text reaches the client already normalised and they have no Kotlin counterpart. A diff confined to those is out of scope here -- verified at v0.8.8-rc3, where normalizeBeforeClosingArtifactFence was rewritten.
entries.failure_mode: An artifact renders as raw source, or swallows the rest of the reply. The corpus test pins current agreement at 22/25 with a known-divergent set, so a genuine drift shows up there -- but only if someone re-runs the corpus against the new upstream.

entries.why: The two errorType values set_memory stringifies into a failed memory artifact's value. They decide which sentence the user is shown -- that the memory store is already full, or that this particular write would overflow it -- and the server sends only the raw key, never a display string. Watched file-level rather than by block: both literals sit inside createMemoryTool's body, and no smaller exported symbol wraps them -- a block anchored on createMemoryTool extracts only its signature and would compare equal across every revision, which is the inert-watch trap check-mirrors.py warns about. Consequence of watching the whole file: unrelated churn reports DRIFT. It did over 91adcf3f..db431210 (registerMemoryTools gained a toolNames field) and was dismissed after verifying both literals byte-identical at each end -- verify the two literals, not the file, before re-investigating a report here.
entries.failure_mode: A renamed or added errorType silently degrades every storage-limit failure to the generic 'Memory Error' label, dropping the token count and the 'delete some memories' instruction that tells the user how to fix it. Nothing errors: the artifact still decodes and a card still renders.

entries.why: Upstream now filters what a Claude model may receive natively through isAnthropicDocumentType, built on this set plus application/pdf. Mobile decides the same question in isProviderCapable, whose anthropic branch is deliberately NARROWER (image/* plus application/pdf only), so a .docx already resolves to UploadRoute.TEXT. The two are the same decision made in two places, and nothing on the wire reconciles them.
entries.failure_mode: Upstream widening what Claude accepts natively leaves mobile extracting text from a file the provider would have read better, or -- if mobile's branch is ever widened to match a stale copy of this list -- routing a type the server now drops. The server console.warns and drops it with no error reaching the client, so a file simply never arrives.

entries.why: MCP tool keys are built as `<toolName>_mcp_<normalizeServerName(server)>`, but GET /api/mcp/servers still advertises the RAW configured name. The client has to normalize identically to write a key any producer will honour; the rule is never served.
entries.failure_mode: A key the server cannot resolve. Upstream surfaces it as 'Tool not found' at execution time -- the save succeeds, the agent looks correct, and every per-tool option (defer_loading, allowed_callers, run_in_background, describe_intent) is silently inert.

entries.why: How many questions an ask_user_question batch may carry. Module-private upstream, never exported and never served, but the resume route rejects a batch outside 1..MAX_QUESTIONS -- so the card truncates the rendered list to it.
entries.failure_mode: Upstream RAISING the cap is the dangerous direction: the card renders the first four of a five-question batch and submits a four-entry answer map, which the route rejects 400 'Answers are required for every question' on BOTH Send and Skip. The run stays paused with Stop as the only escape, and nothing on this side errors or logs.

entries.why: The per-answer character cap the resume route enforces on both the bare and the batched path. Mirrored because the answer boxes budget against it, so a user cannot compose an answer the route will refuse.
entries.failure_mode: Upstream LOWERING it makes a long answer 400 at submit with the run already paused; raising it costs the user characters they were entitled to type. Both are silent -- a stale copy still compiles and still submits.

entries.why: A generation reconciled away is rewritten to an ordinary `event: error` frame for protocol-v1 clients. `final: true` there is a writeEvent option consumed by telemetry, never a body field, and the genuine-error frame on the same route also carries generationProtocolVersion -- so this literal sentence is the only thing on the wire separating a benign reconciliation (the reply is saved; refetch it) from a real stream failure.
entries.failure_mode: Upstream rewording the sentence makes every reconciliation read as a stream error again: the saved reply still loads, but under an alarming error banner, and the run is reported as failed when it was not. Nothing fails to decode.

entries.why: StreamErrorType transcribes the wire strings of upstream's ErrorTypes enum by hand -- the server never serves the table, it only sends one of its values on a stream-error payload. The enum lists only the codes with something actionable to say, so upstream ADDING a member is deliberately not drift; upstream RENAMING one of the listed values is, and nothing on this side can see it happen.
entries.failure_mode: A renamed value stops matching, so that error silently degrades to the generic message -- the user is told something went wrong instead of being told to reattach their files or pick another model. Nothing fails to decode and nothing errors.

entries.why: The MCP save path branches on the literal `MCP_OAUTH_SECRET_REENTRY_REQUIRED` to turn a 400 into a re-enter-your-secret prompt rather than a generic failure. The wire value carries an `MCP_` prefix that upstream's TypeScript member name drops, so the copy cannot be derived from the member name and has to be transcribed.
entries.failure_mode: A renamed code makes the re-entry prompt unreachable: the save reports a plain 'could not save' and the user has no way to learn the stored secret is the thing that must be re-supplied, so the write keeps failing forever.

entries.why: The response bodies that distinguish LibreChat's own terminal 403 on /api/auth/refresh ('Invalid refresh token', 'Invalid OpenID refresh token', 'No session found') from a 403 minted by a reverse proxy, WAF or IP bouncer. Only the former means the session is dead and the tokens should be dropped. NOTE: this watch is deliberately COARSE — the three literals are inline in a ~150-line controller that also carries the OpenID reuse path, the session lookup and its logging, and upstream does not hoist them into a constant to anchor on. So expect it to report on edits that do not touch the literals, and diff the send() arms specifically rather than skimming the block. 'Invalid refresh token' has been confirmed byte-for-byte against a live v0.8.7 (403, text/html, 21 bytes); the other two arms are code-read only.
entries.failure_mode: Upstream rewords an arm and the client stops recognising a dead session: it classifies a real expiry as an intermediary block, keeps the dead tokens and never routes to re-auth. Nothing fails to decode, so a sync's ordinary diff sweep reads it as an inert string edit.

entries.why: banResponse answers 403 with {"message": "Your account has been temporarily banned..."}. The client matches on that wording to tell a genuine account ban from any other 403, because a 403 from a proxy must not end the session.
entries.failure_mode: Upstream rewords the ban sentence and a real ban stops being recognised: the request fails without the session ever being torn down, so the user sits in a broken shell instead of being told they are banned.
